ki_act-grundlagen-01.question: What is the fundamental goal of the EU AI Act?

options.a: It generally bans the use of artificial intelligence for companies in the EU
options.b: It regulates AI systems through a risk-based approach to protect fundamental rights and safety while still enabling innovation
options.c: It sets purely technical standards for software developers with no legal effect on companies
options.d: It completely replaces the GDPR for any data processing that involves AI

ki_act-grundlagen-01.explanation: The AI Act follows a risk-based approach: the greater the risk an AI system poses to safety or fundamental rights, the stricter the requirements. There is no blanket ban on AI, and the regulation does not replace the GDPR - both apply in parallel.

ki_act-grundlagen-02.question: Into how many basic risk tiers does the AI Act classify AI systems?

options.a: Two tiers: allowed and banned
options.b: Five tiers, staggered by industry sector
options.c: Four tiers: unacceptable risk, high risk, limited risk (transparency obligations), and minimal risk
options.d: Three tiers, based purely on company size

ki_act-grundlagen-02.explanation: The core concept of the AI Act is the risk pyramid: unacceptable risk (banned), high risk (strict requirements, e.g. for applicant screening or credit scoring), limited risk (mainly transparency duties, e.g. chatbots), and minimal risk (few obligations, e.g. spam filters or game AI).

ki_act-grundlagen-03.question: According to the Art. 3(1) definition, what is the decisive feature of an 'AI system'?

options.a: It is a machine-based system that operates with some degree of autonomy and infers from inputs how to generate outputs such as content, predictions, recommendations, or decisions
options.b: It must necessarily be based on neural networks or generative AI, otherwise it does not count as an AI system
options.c: It must always run in the cloud; locally installed software never falls under the definition
options.d: It must be marketed by a human as 'AI', otherwise the regulation does not apply

ki_act-grundlagen-03.explanation: The definition is deliberately technology-neutral: what matters is the ability to infer from input data how to generate outputs, regardless of whether a simple rule-based system, machine learning, or a large language model is behind it. A purely fixed, hard-coded rule set without any form of inference generally does not qualify.

ki_act-grundlagen-04.question: Which of the following is a typical example of a 'high-risk AI system' under the AI Act?

options.a: AI that automatically corrects spelling mistakes in emails
options.b: An AI-powered movie recommendation feature in a streaming app
options.c: An AI chatbot answering general product questions in customer service
options.d: AI software that pre-screens job applications and helps decide who gets invited to an interview

ki_act-grundlagen-04.explanation: AI used in HR that helps decide on hiring, promotion, or dismissal is explicitly listed as a high-risk area in Annex III of the AI Act, because it can significantly affect individuals' rights and opportunities. Spell-checking, movie recommendations, and simple chatbots, by contrast, are considered minimal or limited risk.

ki_act-ki_kompetenz-01.question: Who does Article 4 of the AI Act require to ensure sufficient 'AI literacy'?

options.a: Only providers (manufacturers) of AI systems, not the companies that use those systems day to day
options.b: Only large corporations with more than 250 employees
options.c: Both providers and deployers of AI systems - including companies that merely use ready-made AI tools
options.d: Only IT departments, since they are the only ones who technically interact with AI systems

ki_act-ki_kompetenz-01.explanation: Article 4 explicitly addresses both providers (who develop or place AI systems on the market) and deployers, who use AI systems under their own responsibility - for example, a company using a purchased AI tool in customer service. Both groups must ensure their staff have sufficient AI literacy.

ki_act-ki_kompetenz-02.question: According to Article 4, which people within an organisation must have AI literacy ensured for them?

options.a: Only permanent employees, not external contractors or freelancers
options.b: All persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on behalf of the provider or deployer - including staff and other engaged persons
options.c: Only senior management, since they bear ultimate responsibility
options.d: Only people who personally program or train AI models

ki_act-ki_kompetenz-02.explanation: The obligation is deliberately broad and covers not only permanent staff but everyone who deals with AI systems on the company's behalf - this can include freelancers, temporary workers, or external contractors who, for example, use an AI tool in customer contact.

ki_act-ki_kompetenz-03.question: Under Article 4, must AI-literacy training be identical for all employees of a company?

options.a: No - the scope of training should account for people's technical knowledge, experience, education, and the specific context in which they use AI
options.b: Yes - the regulation prescribes one standardised, nationwide curriculum with identical content for every role
options.c: Yes - only a single, company-wide mandatory training with the same exam for everyone satisfies the requirement
options.d: No, training content is entirely optional and does not need to cover risks or practical use at all

ki_act-ki_kompetenz-03.explanation: Article 4 explicitly requires taking into account people's technical knowledge, experience, education, and the context in which the AI systems will be used - training should therefore be tailored to the role. Someone who occasionally uses an AI writing assistant needs different content than someone making AI-supported decisions in a high-risk area.

ki_act-ki_kompetenz-04.question: Since when has the AI-literacy obligation under Article 4 already applied in practice?

options.a: Only from 2 August 2027, at the same time as the strictest high-risk obligations
options.b: Already since 2 February 2025 - alongside the ban on certain AI practices under Article 5
options.c: Only from 2 August 2026, together with most transparency obligations
options.d: The obligation only applies once a company deploys a high-risk AI system as listed in Annex III

ki_act-ki_kompetenz-04.explanation: Under Article 113(a) of the AI Act, Chapter I (including Article 4, AI literacy) and Chapter II (Article 5, prohibited practices) have already applied since 2 February 2025 - well before most of the regulation, which only becomes applicable from 2 August 2026. Any organisation that has ignored the AI-literacy duty so far is therefore already behind, not merely facing a future deadline.

ki_act-verbotene_praktiken-01.question: A company is considering an AI system that rates employees based on their social behaviour and personal traits, producing a general 'trust score' used across quite different contexts (e.g. performance review, access to resources). How is this classified under the AI Act?

options.a: Unproblematic, as long as employees give informal consent
options.b: Banned only in Germany, explicitly allowed in other EU member states
options.c: Allowed as long as the score is not published
options.d: Such cross-context 'social scoring' of people counts as a practice prohibited under Article 5 and may not be deployed anywhere in the EU

ki_act-verbotene_praktiken-01.explanation: Social scoring - evaluating or classifying natural persons over time based on their social behaviour or personal characteristics, leading to detrimental treatment in unrelated contexts - is one of the classic 'red lines' of Article 5 of the AI Act and is banned across the whole EU, regardless of individual consent.

ki_act-verbotene_praktiken-02.question: Using 'real-time' remote biometric identification via AI systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes is, in principle, prohibited under Article 5. Is this true without any exception?

options.a: Yes, there are absolutely no exceptions - any use is banned in every case
options.b: No, private security firms may use it completely freely without restriction
options.c: No, there are narrowly defined exceptions (e.g. targeted search for missing persons, averting a specific terrorist threat) that are subject to strict conditions and usually require prior judicial authorisation
options.d: No, any company may use it as long as it first conducts a data protection impact assessment

ki_act-verbotene_praktiken-02.explanation: The regulation provides narrow, exhaustively listed exceptions for real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes (e.g. searching for a missing child, averting a specific and present terrorist threat), which generally require prior judicial or independent administrative authorisation. For private companies outside law enforcement, such use generally remains prohibited regardless.

ki_act-verbotene_praktiken-03.question: A marketing team wants to deploy an AI system that deliberately uses subliminal techniques, imperceptible to users, to manipulate their purchasing decisions and cause them significant harm. How should this be assessed?

options.a: This falls under the manipulative or deceptive practices prohibited by Article 5, since subliminal techniques are deliberately used to materially distort behaviour with potential for harm
options.b: This is legitimate, creative marketing as long as the terms and conditions mention 'personalised advertising'
options.c: This is only prohibited when targeting children; it is generally permitted for adults
options.d: This does not fall under the AI Act at all, since it is marketing rather than a high-risk system

ki_act-verbotene_praktiken-03.explanation: Article 5 of the AI Act bans AI systems that use subliminal, manipulative, or deceptive techniques beyond a person's conscious awareness to materially distort their behaviour in a way likely to cause significant harm - regardless of whether the target group is children or adults. A note in the terms and conditions does not change this, since the technique specifically targets unconscious influence.

ki_act-verbotene_praktiken-04.question: An AI system is deliberately designed to exploit the vulnerability of elderly people or people in difficult economic circumstances, in order to influence their behaviour to their detriment. How does the AI Act classify this?

options.a: As a high-risk practice that may nonetheless be lawfully used after a conformity assessment
options.b: As one of the practices prohibited under Article 5, since it deliberately exploits vulnerabilities due to age, disability, or social/economic situation in order to act to the detriment of those affected
options.c: As entirely unproblematic, as long as no financial harm occurs
options.d: As a transparency-obligation case where a simple 'You are interacting with an AI' notice is sufficient

ki_act-verbotene_praktiken-04.explanation: Deliberately exploiting the vulnerability of specific groups of people - for example due to age, disability, or a difficult social or economic situation - with the aim of influencing their behaviour to their detriment is one of the practices explicitly banned under Article 5. A conformity assessment or a transparency notice cannot 'cure' such a ban, because prohibited practices cannot be legalised through additional requirements.

ki_act-transparenzpflichten-01.question: Your company uses a chatbot to automatically answer customer queries. What does Article 50 of the AI Act generally require in this case?

options.a: The chatbot must be fully switched off as soon as a customer asks about it
options.b: There is no obligation at all, as long as the chatbot works technically without errors
options.c: Customers must be clearly and timely informed that they are interacting with an AI system rather than a human - unless this is obvious anyway from the circumstances
options.d: The chatbot may only be used after a conformity assessment equivalent to that for high-risk systems has been carried out

ki_act-transparenzpflichten-01.explanation: Article 50 requires systems intended for direct interaction with natural persons to inform users that they are interacting with an AI system - unless this is obvious to a reasonably informed, observant person (e.g. clearly automated standard FAQ bots). A high-risk conformity assessment is not required here, since a simple chatbot is generally not a high-risk system.

ki_act-transparenzpflichten-02.question: A colleague uses an AI image generator to create a realistic-looking video in which a well-known person appears to say things they never actually said ('deepfake'), and wants to distribute it internally and externally. What generally applies here?

options.a: The video must be labelled as AI-generated or manipulated, so viewers can recognise that the content and statements are not authentic
options.b: A labelling duty only applies to commercial use outside the EU
options.c: Deepfakes are categorically banned and may never be created under any circumstances
options.d: There is no labelling obligation as long as no financial profit is made

ki_act-transparenzpflichten-02.explanation: Article 50 of the AI Act requires AI-generated or manipulated image, audio, or video content that falsely appears to depict real people, objects, places, or events ('deepfakes') to be labelled as artificially generated or manipulated. Deepfakes are not banned outright, but they must be made transparent - unlike social scoring, they are not a 'red line' under Article 5, but are instead subject to a labelling obligation.

ki_act-transparenzpflichten-03.question: An emotion-recognition AI system is used in the workplace to gauge employees' mood during meetings. What does Article 50 require at a minimum here?

options.a: Such use is always banned, regardless of context
options.b: The people affected must be informed that an emotion-recognition system is being used
options.c: A note in internal IT documentation is sufficient; informing the affected individuals is not required
options.d: An information duty exists only towards the works council, not towards individual employees

ki_act-transparenzpflichten-03.explanation: For emotion-recognition or biometric-categorisation systems, Article 50 provides for an information duty towards the natural persons exposed to the system - they must be informed that the system is being operated. This does not replace any additional labour-law co-determination rights, such as those of a works council, but applies in addition to them.

ki_act-transparenzpflichten-04.question: From when do the general transparency obligations under Article 50 (e.g. chatbot disclosure, deepfake labelling) become applicable?

options.a: Already since the regulation entered into force in August 2024
options.b: Only from 2 August 2027
options.c: Already since 2 February 2025, together with the prohibited practices
options.d: From 2 August 2026, together with most of the regulation's remaining obligations

ki_act-transparenzpflichten-04.explanation: Unlike the AI-literacy obligation (Article 4) and the prohibited practices (Article 5), which have already applied since 2 February 2025, the Article 50 transparency obligations only take effect on the general application date of 2 August 2026 - together with most of the regulation's remaining obligations. Companies should keep these different deadlines in mind.

ki_act-ki_am_arbeitsplatz-01.question: A colleague wants to paste confidential customer data into a publicly available AI chatbot to get help drafting a reply. What should they consider first?

options.a: This is unproblematic, since AI providers generally never store any input data
options.b: Personal or confidential data generally must not be entered into external AI tools without checking first, since this can violate data-protection rules and internal policy - the GDPR applies here in addition to, and independently of, the AI Act
options.c: This is fine as long as the colleague informally tells the customer about it afterwards
options.d: The AI Act categorically bans any use of external AI chatbots in the workplace

ki_act-ki_am_arbeitsplatz-01.explanation: The AI Act primarily addresses risks arising from the AI system itself, but it does not replace the GDPR. Entering personal or confidential data into an external AI tool can violate data-protection law and internal policy independently of the AI Act, for instance because the data is processed on servers outside the company's control. Both legal frameworks - the AI Act and the GDPR - must be observed in parallel.

ki_act-ki_am_arbeitsplatz-02.question: A high-risk AI system supports the pre-selection of job applications. An employee accepts every AI suggestion without review, reasoning that 'the AI is usually right anyway'. How should this behaviour be assessed against the human-oversight requirements?

options.a: Completely fine, since the AI formally made the decision
options.b: Only a concern if the applicant complains
options.c: Problematic: human oversight for high-risk systems means critically reviewing and being able to justify the AI's suggestions, not rubber-stamping them automatically
options.d: Unproblematic, because the AI's manufacturer bears responsibility for all decisions

ki_act-ki_am_arbeitsplatz-02.explanation: The AI Act requires effective human oversight for high-risk systems: the responsible person must be able to understand, critically question, and, where necessary, correct or override the AI's output (avoiding 'automation bias'). Blindly accepting AI suggestions contradicts this principle and can result in discriminatory decisions, for which the company remains responsible.

ki_act-ki_am_arbeitsplatz-03.question: A manager makes an adverse HR decision based on an AI recommendation, which later turns out to be flawed and discriminatory. The manager argues: 'The AI suggested it, I just went along with it.' Is this argument legally sound?

options.a: No - responsibility for a decision generally remains with the human, or with the company as the deployer using the AI system; 'the AI said so' does not remove the duty of care
options.b: Yes - as soon as an AI system issues a recommendation, full legal responsibility automatically shifts to the AI's manufacturer
options.c: Yes, but only if the company has fewer than 50 employees
options.d: This is legally irrelevant, since the AI Act contains no provisions on deployer responsibilities

ki_act-ki_am_arbeitsplatz-03.explanation: The AI Act imposes obligations on deployers of high-risk AI systems, including exercising appropriate human oversight and using the system in line with the provider's instructions. These duties - and the resulting responsibility for concrete decisions made in the business - generally remain with the company or the acting individual, even where an AI provided the underlying recommendation.

ki_act-ki_am_arbeitsplatz-04.question: What is a sensible, practical rule of thumb for using generative AI assistants (e.g. for drafting text) in everyday work?

options.a: Always use AI-generated text unchanged and unreviewed to save time
options.b: Review AI-generated output for content before using it - especially for accuracy, bias, and data-protection concerns - and check against applicable internal policy when in doubt
options.c: Only ever use generative AI outside working hours and with no work relevance whatsoever
options.d: Skip any review entirely as long as no customer sees the content directly

ki_act-ki_am_arbeitsplatz-04.explanation: Generative AI can be very useful at work, but it does not replace one's own professional and legal responsibility. Outputs can be factually wrong ('hallucinations'), contain unintended bias, or raise data-protection concerns if confidential information was accidentally entered - so a critical review before further use is good workplace practice.

ki_act-grundlagen-05.question: A company develops and uses an AI system exclusively for national military defence purposes. Does the AI Act apply to it?

options.a: No - under Art. 2(3), the AI Act does not apply to AI systems placed on the market, put into service or used exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes
options.b: Yes, without restriction - military use is expressly listed as its own high-risk area in Annex III
options.c: No, but only if the system has additionally been officially certified by NATO
options.d: Yes, but at least the transparency obligations under Art. 50 still fully apply regardless

ki_act-grundlagen-05.explanation: Art. 2(3) fully excludes AI systems intended exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes from the Regulation's scope, regardless of which type of entity operates them. There is no separate NATO certification for this, and the transparency obligations also do not apply in this case.

ki_act-grundlagen-06.question: A research team develops and tests a new AI model purely for scientific research purposes, before it is ever placed on the market or put into service. How is this classified under the AI Act?

options.a: Such research, testing and development activity prior to being placed on the market or put into service generally falls outside the scope of the Regulation
options.b: Even pure research must first undergo a full conformity assessment as if it were a high-risk system
options.c: The exemption only applies if the research is carried out at a public university, not in the private sector
options.d: The exemption continues to apply unchanged once the model is subsequently made available to real users on the market

ki_act-grundlagen-06.explanation: Art. 2(8) excludes research, testing and development activity regarding AI systems or models prior to their being placed on the market or put into service from the scope of the Regulation. The exemption is not limited to public institutions, but it ends once the system is actually made available on the market or put into service - from that point the regular obligations apply.

ki_act-grundlagen-07.question: According to the definition in Art. 3(3) of the AI Act, who counts as a 'provider' of an AI system?

options.a: Only a natural person who personally writes the program code for an AI system
options.b: Any natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body that develops an AI system or has one developed, and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark - whether for payment or free of charge
options.c: Exclusively companies established outside the EU that export AI systems into the EU
options.d: Any company that merely uses a finished AI tool built by a third party within its own operations, without passing it on further

ki_act-grundlagen-07.explanation: The provider definition is deliberately broad and does not depend on where the company is established or whether payment is involved, but on whether someone develops (or has developed) an AI system and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark. Option d instead describes more the role of a deployer, who merely uses a system built by someone else.

ki_act-grundlagen-08.question: Besides the list in Annex III, there is a second, independent way an AI system can become high-risk. Which one is it?

options.a: When the AI system is itself a product, or is a safety component of a product, that is covered by the EU product safety legislation listed in Annex I (e.g. machinery, medical devices), and that product requires third-party conformity assessment
options.b: When the company deploying the AI has more than 500 employees
options.c: When the AI system is deployed simultaneously in more than three EU member states
options.d: When the AI system is offered publicly and free of charge on the internet

ki_act-grundlagen-08.explanation: Art. 6(1) opens up, alongside the application-based classification via Annex III, a second, product-based route: if the AI system is itself a product or a safety component of a product that already falls under existing EU product safety legislation (Annex I, e.g. the Machinery Regulation, the Medical Devices Regulation) and requires third-party conformity assessment there, the AI system is likewise considered high-risk.

ki_act-ki_kompetenz-05.question: How does Art. 3(56) of the AI Act define the term 'AI literacy'?

options.a: As the skills, knowledge and understanding that allow providers, deployers and affected persons to make an informed deployment of AI systems and to gain awareness of the opportunities and risks of AI and the harm it can cause
options.b: As a formal certification that may only be awarded by state-accredited testing bodies
options.c: As purely technical knowledge of programming languages, relevant only to IT specialists
options.d: As a legal obligation to document a fixed minimum number of training hours every year

ki_act-ki_kompetenz-05.explanation: The definition in Art. 3(56) is deliberately broad: it is not about a specific certification or pure programming knowledge, but about skills, knowledge and understanding that enable informed decisions when dealing with AI and create awareness of opportunities, risks and possible harm.

ki_act-ki_kompetenz-06.question: According to Recital 20 of the AI Act, who should AI literacy ultimately also benefit - beyond the providers' and deployers' own staff?

options.a: Exclusively senior management, so they can make sound investment decisions
options.b: Also persons affected by AI-assisted decisions, so they can understand how decisions taken with the assistance of AI affect them
options.c: Exclusively national market surveillance authorities that monitor compliance with the Regulation
options.d: Only external software developers who are contracted to train new AI models

ki_act-ki_kompetenz-06.explanation: Recital 20 of the AI Act makes clear that AI literacy should not only serve providers and deployers themselves, but should also give affected persons the knowledge necessary to understand how decisions taken with the assistance of AI will have an impact on them.

ki_act-ki_kompetenz-07.question: Does Art. 4 of the AI Act require a specific, legally prescribed training format (e.g. a certified exam) for AI literacy?

options.a: No - the wording obliges providers and deployers to take appropriate measures 'to their best extent'; Art. 4 does not prescribe any particular format or certification
options.b: Yes, it must necessarily be a multi-day in-person training with an external certificate
options.c: Yes, only a state-recognised e-learning course satisfies the requirements of Art. 4
options.d: Yes, but only for companies that also provide high-risk AI systems

ki_act-ki_kompetenz-07.explanation: Art. 4 of the AI Act is phrased as a best-efforts obligation ('to their best extent'), not as an obligation of result with a prescribed format. The law leaves open what the concrete measures look like - as long as they are appropriate and take into account prior knowledge, context, and the groups of people affected.

ki_act-ki_kompetenz-08.question: A company only uses a minimal-risk AI system (e.g. an AI-based spell checker), but no high-risk system. Does it still need to comply with Art. 4 of the AI Act on AI literacy?

options.a: Yes - the AI literacy obligation applies to providers and deployers regardless of the risk class of the AI system they actually deploy, not only to high-risk systems
options.b: No, Art. 4 applies exclusively to providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems under Annex III
options.c: No, the obligation only kicks in once the company has more than 50 different AI applications in use
options.d: No, for minimal-risk systems only the transparency obligation under Art. 50 applies, not Art. 4

ki_act-ki_kompetenz-08.explanation: Art. 4 of the AI Act is not limited to high-risk systems but applies to 'AI systems' generally. A company therefore cannot argue that it only uses low-risk tools to exempt itself from the AI literacy obligation - a common but incorrect assumption with real compliance risk.

ki_act-verbotene_praktiken-05.question: An authority wants to use an AI system that predicts a person's risk of committing a future crime based solely on profiling and personality traits, in order to derive measures from this. How is this assessed under the AI Act?

options.a: Such AI-based 'predictive policing', which bases the crime prediction solely on profiling or personality traits, counts as one of the prohibited practices under Art. 5(1)(d)
options.b: This is permitted as long as an official formally signs off on the measure suggested by the AI at the end
options.c: This is an ordinary high-risk system that may be freely used after a conformity assessment
options.d: This is generally permissible, because supporting a human assessment of concrete criminal offences based on objective, verifiable facts is generally prohibited

ki_act-verbotene_praktiken-05.explanation: Art. 5(1)(d) of the AI Act prohibits risk assessments or predictions of a person's criminal propensity based solely on profiling or personality traits. What remains permissible, however, is AI support for a human assessment based on objective, verifiable facts directly linked to concrete criminal conduct - that is the narrow exception, not the default rule.

ki_act-verbotene_praktiken-06.question: A provider wants to build a facial recognition database by automatically and indiscriminately collecting facial images from the open internet and from CCTV footage. How does the AI Act classify this?

options.a: The untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or from CCTV footage to create or expand facial recognition databases counts as a prohibited practice under Art. 5(1)(e)
options.b: This is permitted as long as the collected images are subsequently stored pseudonymously
options.c: This is only prohibited for images of minors, and generally permitted for adults
options.d: This does not fall under the AI Act at all, since it formally constitutes a database rather than a standalone AI system

ki_act-verbotene_praktiken-06.explanation: Art. 5(1)(e) of the AI Act specifically prohibits the untargeted collection of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage to create or expand facial recognition databases - regardless of pseudonymisation or the age of the people depicted. The underlying collection and processing logic falls under the AI Act, even if the end result is formally 'just' a database.

ki_act-verbotene_praktiken-07.question: A school wants to use an AI system that uses camera and microphone input to detect and evaluate students' emotions during lessons - not for medical or safety reasons. How is this assessed under the AI Act?

options.a: Using emotion recognition in educational institutions outside of medical or safety-related reasons counts as one of the prohibited practices under Art. 5(1)(f)
options.b: This is always permitted as long as the school discloses the emotion recognition in line with Art. 50 of the AI Act
options.c: This is only prohibited if the collected results are later published
options.d: This is only prohibited in the workplace, while it is generally permitted in educational institutions

ki_act-verbotene_praktiken-07.explanation: Art. 5(1)(f) of the AI Act prohibits the use of emotion recognition systems both in the workplace and in educational institutions, unless there are medical or safety-related reasons (e.g. detecting fatigue in safety-critical activities). Mere disclosure under Art. 50 of the AI Act is not sufficient here - the ban applies regardless of whether transparent information is provided.

ki_act-verbotene_praktiken-08.question: A company wants to use an AI system that automatically infers a person's presumed sexual orientation, political opinion, or religious belief from biometric data (e.g. facial or voice recognition). How is this classified?

options.a: Such biometric categorisation to infer particularly sensitive attributes such as sexual orientation, political opinion, or religious belief counts as a prohibited practice under Art. 5(1)(g)
options.b: This is permitted as long as the affected person has previously accepted a general privacy notice
options.c: This is generally permitted if it is done exclusively for marketing purposes
options.d: This is only prohibited if the inferred attributes are subsequently resold to third parties

ki_act-verbotene_praktiken-08.explanation: Art. 5(1)(g) of the AI Act prohibits biometric categorisation of natural persons in order to deduce their race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life, or sexual orientation. An accepted privacy notice or a marketing purpose does not change this - narrow exceptions exist only for lawful labelling/filtering of datasets or biometric categorisation by law enforcement authorities.

ki_act-transparenzpflichten-05.question: Your company uses a generative AI system that automatically produces image and text content. What does Art. 50(2) of the AI Act require from the provider of such a system in this regard?

options.a: The provider must ensure that the generated outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, as far as this is technically feasible
options.b: The provider must have every generated piece of content approved by a national supervisory authority before publication
options.c: There is no marking obligation as long as the content is not used commercially
options.d: The marking obligation only applies to video content, not to text or images

ki_act-transparenzpflichten-05.explanation: Art. 50(2) of the AI Act obliges providers of AI systems that generate synthetic image, audio, video, or text content to ensure that these outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, as far as this is technically feasible - regardless of prior approval by authorities or commercial use.

ki_act-transparenzpflichten-06.question: Does the obligation under Art. 50(1) of the AI Act to inform persons that they are interacting with an AI system apply without any exception to every system?

options.a: No - among other things, the obligation does not apply to AI systems legally authorised to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights of third parties - unless the system is available for the public to report a criminal offence
options.b: Yes, there is no exception whatsoever - every AI system must always identify itself in every case
options.c: No, the obligation generally does not apply to any public authority, regardless of the purpose of use
options.d: No, the obligation only applies to AI systems that are offered for a fee

ki_act-transparenzpflichten-06.explanation: Art. 50(1) of the AI Act provides a limited exception for AI systems legally authorised to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights of third parties. However, this exception does not apply where the system is available for the public to report a criminal offence - there, the information obligation still applies. There is no blanket exemption for all public authorities.

ki_act-transparenzpflichten-07.question: A newsroom uses generative AI to create and publish a text on a matter of public interest. However, the text undergoes editorial revision before publication, and a person bears editorial responsibility for it. Must it still be disclosed that AI was involved?

options.a: No - if such a text undergoes a process of human review or editorial control and a person holds editorial responsibility for it, the disclosure obligation under Art. 50(4), second subparagraph, does not apply
options.b: Yes, under the AI Act every use of generative AI in journalistic texts must be disclosed without exception
options.c: No, because journalistic content is generally fully excluded from the scope of the AI Act
options.d: Yes, but only if the published text is longer than 1,000 words

ki_act-transparenzpflichten-07.explanation: Art. 50(4), second subparagraph, of the AI Act generally provides for a disclosure obligation for AI-generated or manipulated text published on matters of public interest. This obligation does not apply, however, where the content has undergone a process of human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for the publication.

ki_act-transparenzpflichten-08.question: Your company uses a high-risk AI system that also falls under the transparency obligations of Art. 50 of the AI Act (e.g. because it interacts directly with people). Do the obligations under Art. 50 and the high-risk obligations under Chapter III mutually exclude each other?

options.a: No - Art. 50(6) clarifies that the transparency obligations do not affect the requirements under Chapter III; both sets of obligations can apply side by side and must be met cumulatively
options.b: Yes, once a system counts as a high-risk system, the Chapter III obligations automatically replace all transparency obligations under Art. 50
options.c: Yes, Art. 50 generally only applies to minimal-risk systems, never to high-risk systems
options.d: No, but only the stricter of the two sets of obligations needs to be met, not both at the same time

ki_act-transparenzpflichten-08.explanation: Art. 50(6) of the AI Act expressly clarifies that the transparency obligations of paragraphs 1 to 4 do not affect the requirements and obligations under Chapter III (high-risk systems). A high-risk system that also falls within the scope of Art. 50 must therefore fulfil both sets of obligations cumulatively, not just one of them.

ki_act-ki_am_arbeitsplatz-05.question: A company wants to introduce a high-risk AI system for evaluating employee performance. What does Art. 26(7) of the AI Act require from an employer acting as deployer before the system is used at the workplace?

options.a: The employer must inform the workers' representatives and the affected employees that they will be subject to the use of the high-risk AI system, before it is put into service or used
options.b: It is sufficient to provide the information retroactively after the first three months of use have passed
options.c: Information is only required if more than 50 employees are affected by the deployment
options.d: It is sufficient to mention the system in the company's general privacy notice, without specifically informing the employees

ki_act-ki_am_arbeitsplatz-05.explanation: Art. 26(7) of the AI Act obliges employers who, as deployers, use a high-risk AI system at the workplace to inform the workers' representatives and the affected employees in advance - not only afterwards, regardless of company size, and not merely in a general privacy notice.

ki_act-ki_am_arbeitsplatz-06.question: Which of the following applications is explicitly listed under Annex III point 4 of the AI Act as a high-risk area for 'employment, workers management and access to self-employment'?

options.a: AI software that automatically allocates tasks to employees or continuously monitors and evaluates their performance and behaviour
options.b: An AI-based canteen app that suggests vegetarian menu options to employees
options.c: AI that automatically corrects spelling mistakes in employees' internal emails
options.d: An AI-based time-tracking app that exclusively logs attendance, without any evaluation of performance

ki_act-ki_am_arbeitsplatz-06.explanation: Annex III point 4(b) of the AI Act explicitly names AI systems that make decisions on working conditions, promotion or termination, allocate tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits, or continuously monitor and evaluate the performance and behaviour of employees. Purely administrative tools without an evaluative function (canteen app, spell checker, plain attendance logging) do not fall under this.

ki_act-ki_am_arbeitsplatz-07.question: A high-risk AI system for pre-screening job applications is to be used within a company. What must the system itself, according to Art. 14(4) of the AI Act, technically enable for the persons assigned to human oversight?

options.a: It must be designed so that the overseeing person can monitor its operation, correctly interpret its output, decide against using it or ignore, override or reverse the output, and interrupt its operation via a 'stop' button or similar procedure
options.b: It must be designed so that it can only be shut down remotely by the manufacturer, not by the deploying company
options.c: It is sufficient for a person to spot-check the system logs once a year
options.d: It must be designed so that the system's decisions can never be reversed, in order to prevent subsequent manipulation

ki_act-ki_am_arbeitsplatz-07.explanation: Art. 14(4) of the AI Act requires high-risk AI systems to be designed so that the person assigned to oversight understands the system's capacities and limitations, can correctly interpret its outputs, can decide against using it or ignore, override or reverse the output, and can interrupt its operation via a 'stop' button or a similar procedure. An annual spot-check or a shutdown capability held exclusively by the manufacturer does not meet this requirement.

ki_act-ki_am_arbeitsplatz-08.question: An AI system, without any human involvement, makes the final decision to reject a job applicant, based solely on an automated evaluation of her application documents. What additional right can the applicant assert independently of the AI Act?

options.a: The right under Art. 22 GDPR not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing that produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects her, subject to the exceptions set out there
options.b: A right to immediate hiring, regardless of the substantive outcome of the application
options.c: The right to have the AI software's manufacturer disclose the complete source code to her
options.d: There is no additional right, because the AI Act fully displaces the GDPR in employment matters

ki_act-ki_am_arbeitsplatz-08.explanation: The AI Act primarily regulates risks arising from the AI system itself and does not replace the GDPR. In parallel, Art. 22 GDPR grants affected persons the right not to be subject solely to an automated decision that produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects them - such as a fully automated job rejection without any human involvement, subject to the narrow exceptions specified in the law.
